query: For MnNiSi-based magnetic-refrigeration materials, what single intervention could improve mechanical performance while retaining a large magnetocaloric effect? Formulate one hypothesis that specifies the intervention, its proposed mechanism, the expected changes relative to an appropriate baseline, the conditions under which it should hold, supporting prior evidence, and an experiment whose result would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Replacing a portion of Ni with up to ~10 atomic percent Fe in MnNiSi-based alloys will improve mechanical toughness while preserving the large magnetocaloric effect, by enhancing structural stability without significantly altering the magnetostructural transition.
generation.material_initial_state: MnNiSi-based alloy prepared by standard casting or melting routes (prior to any compositional modifications).
generation.intervention: Partial substitution of Ni by up to ~10 atomic percent Fe in the MnNiSi-based compound, followed by homogenization annealing.
generation.conditions: Preparation via arc melting under inert atmosphere and post-annealing at ~900 °C, characterization of properties in the 300–400 K range.
generation.structural_mediator: Enhanced phase stability due to Fe doping in the lattice, reducing brittleness while retaining the magnetostructural transition.
generation.mechanism: Fe substitution modifies the bonding environment and stabilizes microstructural features that increase mechanical robustness with minimal impact on the entropy change associated with the magnetocaloric effect.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the undoped MnNiSi baseline, the Fe-substituted alloys will exhibit higher fracture toughness or an improved mechanical strength–ductility balance while retaining a comparable peak magnetocaloric response in the operating temperature range.
generation.baseline: Undoped MnNiSi alloy produced under similar conditions, measured in the same temperature and magnetic field range.
generation.boundary: Exceeding ~10 atomic percent Fe or altering the annealing protocol could degrade the magnetocaloric performance or induce secondary phases that compromise mechanical improvement.
generation.uncertainty: Direct evidence specific to MnNiSi–Fe cannot be confirmed from these references alone, so there is moderate confidence in the expected magnitude of improvement.

falsification_experiment.design: Synthesize a series of MnNi1−xFexSi alloys with 0 ≤ x ≤ 0.10 via arc melting, homogenize at ~900 °C, then measure mechanical properties and magnetocaloric performance from 300 K to 400 K.
measurements: Tensile or compression tests to quantify yield strength and ductility
Magnetization and heat capacity measurements to determine the magnetocaloric effect (ΔS and ΔT)
Phase analysis (X-ray diffraction) and microstructure observation (SEM/TEM)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the partially Fe-substituted samples fail to show both an improvement in mechanical performance relative to undoped MnNiSi and a comparable peak magnetocaloric effect (within 10% of the baseline ΔS), then the hypothesis is falsified.

In this spirit, the properties of conventional SMMs are also included in the property chart for comparison. The HEAs of this work show excellent values of yield and ultimate tensile strength which outperform those of other SMMs, yet preserving good coercivity, with values below 11 Oe (0.87 kA m−1). Figure 3e shows the saturation magnetization of the investigated alloys at high temperatures up to 873 K, suggesting that the magnetic properties of the HEAs also have good temperature resistance. The so-called “high entropy alloys” (HEAs) are a class of emergent transition metal alloys that hold great potential for advanced manufacturing, and which may impact magnetocalorics. These are near equimolar alloys with high entropy of mixing when in a random solid solution. These materials have been pursued for high hardness and resistance to wear and corrosion, which are attractive properties for a myriad of applications. Fe1Co1Ni1Cr1Pdx is an example HEA system with tunable magnetic properties. The addition of Pd was shown to change the critical temperature (Tc) from 300 to 500 K for x = 1 to 2, along with enhancement of the saturation magnetization; previous works have used high percentages of Pd as a stabilizing agent in similar high strength bulk alloys. In this work, we explore the magnetic properties of the Fe1Co1Ni1Cr1Pdx alloy family, as-rolled and after annealing, with low molar fractions of Pd. We find improvement in the magnetocaloric properties throughout the system. A detailed statistical analysis of the universal scaling behavior suggest this originates predominately from the homogenization of the alloy with both Pd and heat treatment. occupying_moves.conditions: doping up to ~10% Fe in Ni sites, typical vacuum or inert atmosphere, post-annealing at ~900°C

chosen.conditions: 0–10 at.% Fe doping, measured from 300–400 K for magnetocaloric and mechanical properties
chosen.why: We hypothesize that partially replacing Ni with Fe in MnNiSi-based alloys enhances mechanical toughness by reducing brittleness through improved structural stability, while preserving the large magnetocaloric effect by maintaining magnetostructural compatibility. Prior evidence indicates that Fe doping in Mn-based systems can bolster ductility without significantly degrading their magnetic performance. To test this, we propose preparing MnNi1–xFexSi alloys with up to ~10 at.% Fe via arc melting and homogenization, then measuring magnetization, heat capacity, and mechanical strength. A failure to maintain both the large magnetocaloric response and improved mechanical properties would falsify this hypothesis.
